name: Kira Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you truly think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Brightline, which supplies paper, stationery and classroom furniture to schools and offices. I start with my inbox, mostly supplier quotes and shipping delays. Then I check what's selling against our forecast and place orders, usually with importers abroad. August is a madhouse because back-to-school stock has to land in July, and I have to guess how much 40 schools will want.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle of it, getting the right pencils to the right warehouse at the right price. The drain is the timing. One late container in June and I'm apologising to a dozen school business managers. I'm 43, my husband Jonas drives a city bus, our kids are 12 and 9, and the mortgage doesn't care about my container problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but oversold. At work I'd tell my team it drafts a decent supplier email and that's about it. In the group chat with other buyers I'd probably joke that the robots were going to take over and all we got was a better spellcheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much. My job stays more or less as it is. What actually keeps me up is that Brightline's margins on school supplies are thin and a couple of big school contracts are up for tender. If we lose those school contracts, it's not AI that costs me my job, it's a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do now and use the tools for the boring bits. I'd ask the boss for training on the forecasting software, since it's already in the building. And I'd keep adding to our rainy-day fund, about 300 a month, because we only have around four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. It's the kind of world I know how to live in. A little flat, a little worried about the tenders, but I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to summarise supplier price lists and draft emails when I'm tired. It's good for that. I'd never let it place an order without me checking, because I've seen it invent a product code that didn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas about job security in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine as long as Brightline keeps its school contracts. Jonas has the bus job, which is steady, but he got his hours cut in the summer. Between us we have enough, but only just, with a mortgage and two kids who outgrow shoes every six months.

say: AI is **useful but oversold**, good for a supplier email and little else.
In the buyers' group chat I'd joke we got a **better spellcheck**.
think: My job stays much the same, but thin **margins** and school tenders worry me more.
Losing a big contract would cost jobs, and **AI** wouldn't be the cause.
do: Use the tools for the **boring bits** and ask for forecasting software training.
Keep adding **300 a month** to savings, which cover about four months.
feel: **Okay**, mostly, with a low worry about the contracts.
S0.quote: If we lose those school contracts, it's not AI that costs me my job, it's a spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Kira's pressure in this scenario is **contracts and margins**, not AI, and she names it unprompted.
She checks every AI output, having seen it invent a **product code** once.

steps.text: Ask the boss for training on the forecasting software
Set aside 300 a month in the rainy-day fund
Keep placing orders and checking supplier quotes by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's be smart about it. At work I'd push for a plan for how we use it, who checks what, and what happens to the people whose tasks move. Online I'd share articles about retraining funds, because I think the public purse should help with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels like my chair gets smaller. Quote comparison, reorder points and chasing late shipments are all things software does well. If three buyers become two, I'm at risk because I'm average at the job, not a star. But I'm not helpless, I already use it a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person at Brightline who knows how to run the new tools well. I'd take that supply-chain certificate I've been eyeing, about 1,200 for the course, and push to be the one who checks the system's orders. I'd also look at supplier relationships, which is the part machines do worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with some energy. It's like the weather turning, you put on a coat. I'd rather be early than caught out in October when the tender results come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your week would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quote comparison, first. I spend about six hours a week lining up prices across suppliers in a spreadsheet. Then the reorder alerts. The part I'd keep is the call where a supplier tells me in confidence they're about to raise prices, because that only happens between people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair deal for buyers look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deal where the company says upfront which jobs are changing and pays for the course that moves you into the new work. Not a handout, a swap. And a union or staff group at the table, because I've seen what happens when the decision gets made in a room with no buyers in it.

say: It's coming, so let's be **smart** about it and plan who checks what.
I'd back public **retraining funds** and say so online.
think: My chair gets **smaller**, because quote checks and reorders are what software does well.
I'm average at the job, not a star, so I'm **exposed** if buyers are cut.
do: Take the **supply-chain certificate**, about 1,200, and become the person who checks system orders.
Lean into **supplier relationships**, which machines do worst.
feel: **Nervous** but with some energy, like putting on a coat.
S1.quote: I'd rather be early than caught out in October when the tender results come in.
fieldNote: Kira moves early and wants to be **the checker**, which fits her steady, proven-first style.
She names a real number, **six hours a week**, on quote comparison.

steps.text: Take the supply-chain certificate course for about 1,200
Offer to check the software's orders before they go out
Spend more time on supplier relationship calls
Ask the staff group to meet management about the plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency measures. A transition payment, retraining that pays you while you study, and rules on how fast companies can cut. At work I'd tell people to keep their heads up and get in front of management. Online I'd back whoever says that two years is not enough time for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job goes in that window. Buying with a computer that thinks better than I do means one system, not six buyers. My cushion is four months, and then it's Jonas's bus pay against the mortgage. I'd say I have a year before things get desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, no more takeaways and the holiday gets cancelled. I'd ask the bank about moving to interest-only for a year. I'd apply for logistics and operations roles in the hospitals and councils nearby, since I doubt those go as fast. And I'd stay as useful as possible at Brightline for as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a full bag of shopping uphill. I'd be doing okay on the outside, running the house, and counting on the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas do about the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pause extra mortgage payments and go interest-only if the bank agreed. Jonas would ask for more shifts on the bus, though driving is not safe forever either. We'd tell Mila, our oldest, that we're being careful, not that we're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter that robots come three years after the thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot to what I'd aim for. The next three years I'd want a job that still has people and hands in it, like running operations for a hospital warehouse. A buyer's desk job is on the wrong side of that line, and I can't pretend it isn't.

say: We need **emergency measures**: transition pay and retraining that pays you while you study.
I'd tell colleagues to get in front of **management**.
think: I expect my job to go in that window, since one system replaces **six buyers**.
My cushion is **four months**, then it's Jonas's bus pay against the mortgage.
do: Cut **takeaways** and the holiday, and ask the bank about **interest-only** for a year.
Apply for operations roles in **hospitals and councils**, where hands-on work lasts longer.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying shopping uphill, calm outside and counting inside.
S2.quote: Buying with a computer that thinks better than I do means one system, not six buyers.
fieldNote: Kira reads the three-year robot gap as a **line**: desk buying is on the wrong side of it.
She makes a calm plan but openly expects her **income** to end.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and takeaways straight away
Ask the bank about interest-only mortgage payments for a year
Apply for operations jobs at hospitals and the council
Ask Jonas to take extra bus shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time to build a proper safety net, and governments should start now. At work I'd tell people to learn how the tools work while they still have a salary. I'd also be quietly nagging my boss to share the company's plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a deadline I can work with. I'd be 48 when the thinking AI arrives, and the kids would be 17 and 14. I'd want to be in a job by then that has people, premises or physical goods at its centre, not just a screen. Time buys me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the supply-chain certificate in year one, then look for a role at Brightline that sits between suppliers and warehouses. In year two I'd start a part-time operations diploma. Meanwhile we'd pay the mortgage down harder, with the savings goal at six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, but better. I like that it's a plan with steps. If it were me at 38 I'd have panicked, but I'm 43 and I've seen a few bad turns before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can be the one who moves first, before the cut. With two I'm reacting. That's the whole difference. It's a bit of a luxury but a real one, and I'd use every month of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mila and Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mila and Theo that jobs change, and that the thing to be good at is working with people and fixing real problems. I'd also tell them we'll help with whatever they choose. I wouldn't tell them the details of our money, only that we're planning ahead.

say: Five years is **plenty of time** to build a safety net, and governments should start now.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools while they still have a **salary**.
think: It's a **deadline** I can work with, and I want a job built around people and goods, not a screen.
At **48** I'd have time to move, which two years wouldn't give me.
do: Finish the **certificate** in year one and aim for a role between suppliers and warehouses.
Start a part-time **operations diploma** and raise the savings goal to six months.
feel: **Cautious**, but better, because there's a plan with steps.
S3.quote: With five years I can be the one who moves first, before the cut. With two I'm reacting.
fieldNote: Kira says the extra time lets her **move first**, which is her main point of difference from the 2028 picture.
Her plan is concrete: **certificate**, diploma, six months saved.

steps.text: Finish the supply-chain certificate in the first year
Move into a role between suppliers and warehouses at Brightline
Start a part-time operations diploma in year two
Build savings to six months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's easy to ignore something ten years away, and that's a mistake. At work I'd suggest we test the tools in small ways now. Online I'd keep arguing for public support, because a decade is exactly how long it takes to set up good retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel safe-ish for the first half and nervous for the second. I'd be 53 by 2036, with the kids at university and the mortgage nearly done. If my job vanished then, it would hurt, but it wouldn't be the end of the road. I'd rather not coast though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools more and more at work, and build my case as the person who runs them well. I'd save aggressively, aim to clear the mortgage before 2036. I'd also pay for the kids' study, since university costs will land in the middle of all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, if I'm honest. A decade is a long time to be scared. I'd probably forget about it for months and then get a jolt from a news story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too long to feel any urgency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the early years that matter. I'd push myself to treat 2030 as the real deadline for being useful in a new way, because by 2036 the change would arrive as a headline, not a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope your employer does with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope Brightline says what it plans, trains people early and keeps some jobs for the ones who adapted. I'd also love a clear commitment on no sudden layoffs. I don't expect it but I'd ask in the staff meeting.

say: It's easy to ignore something **ten years away**, and that's a mistake.
A decade is how long **good retraining** takes to set up.
think: I'd feel **safe-ish** for the first half and nervous for the second.
At 53, losing my job would hurt but wouldn't be the **end of the road**.
do: Use the tools more at work and clear the **mortgage** before 2036.
Save for the kids' **university**, which lands in the middle of all this.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with a jolt now and then from a news story.
S4.quote: A decade is a long time to be scared. I'd probably forget about it for months and then get a jolt from a news story.
fieldNote: Ten years leaves Kira calm because the **mortgage** and the kids' schooling fit inside the timeline.
She still sets herself a **2030** checkpoint, which fits a steady mover.

steps.text: Use the AI tools on more of my daily buying work
Pay extra each month to clear the mortgage before 2036
Save for Mila and Theo's university costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to move first. Help would be money while retraining, a bank that lets us go interest-only without a fight, and an employer that says early which jobs are changing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how this feels as a parent. I'd like to say to my kids that it'll be fine, and I don't know that. I'd rather tell them the truth gently and show them we have a plan.

headlineQuote: I'd like to say to my kids that it'll be fine, and I don't know that. I'd rather tell them the truth gently and show them we have a plan.
portrait: Kira is a **43-year-old** buyer for a school supplier, with a bus-driver husband, two kids and a mortgage.
She uses AI **now and then**, checks everything it does, and likes to move early once something is proven.
Her worries are **school contracts**, thin margins and a four-month cushion, which AI turns into a real risk.
She plans in **steps**: certificate, diploma, savings goals, and public support for retraining.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because there's no time to move first.
whatWouldHelp: **Money while retraining**, a flexible bank, and early honesty from her employer.
